12235               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
12236               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
12237               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
12238               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
12239               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
12240               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
12241               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
12242               	; 	'
12243               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
12244               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
12245               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
12246               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
12247               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
12248               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
12249               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.
12250               	; 	escp = escp + 1

12263               	; 	#if NES
12264               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
12265               	; 	'
12266               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
12267               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
12268               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
12269               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
12270               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
12271               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
12272               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
12273               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
12274               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
12275               	; 	'
12276               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
12277               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
12278               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
12279               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
12280               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
12281               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
12282               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
12283               	; 	'
12284               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
12285               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
12286               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
12287               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
12288               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
12289               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
12290               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
12291               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
12292               	; 	' with room to spare.
12293               	; 	'
12294               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
12295               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
12296               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
12297               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
12298               	; 	WAIT
12299               	; 	#endif

12303               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
12304               	; 	' 7 an east one.
12305               	; 	'
12306               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
12307               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
12308               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character

12310               	; 	'
12311               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO

12647               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------- the scanner's furniture
12648               	; 	' Without this the scanner is two dots in a void: you can see THAT Harry is
12649               	; 	' somewhere, but not what he is near, which is the one thing you actually
12650               	; 	' need when he is off-screen. Floor lines say which level, the slashes say
12651               	; 	' where that floor's escalator is, and the bar says where the elevator is --
12652               	; 	' exactly the three things the manual lists.
12653               	; 	'
12654               	; 	' FURNITURE AND DOTS ARE SEGREGATED BY PIXEL ROW ON PURPOSE, and a level
12655               	; 	' band is now FOUR rows, one per colour, because a pixel row carries
12656               	; 	' exactly one colour here:
12657               	; 	'
12658               	; 	'   +0  GREY    escalator head, and the elevator car
12659               	; 	'   +1  GREY    the air of that floor
12660               	; 	'   +2  GREY
12661               	; 	'   +3  YELLOW  the floor line -- and NOTHING else goes here
12662               	; 	'
12663               	; 	' THE FIRST THREE ROWS ARE THE FLOOR'S AIR AND EVERYTHING LIVES IN THEM:
12664               	; 	' the escalator's three-step diagonal, the lift car, and both actors, all
12665               	; 	' three pixels tall. They are grey in the table, and the Kop and the
12666               	; 	' crook recolour their own CHARACTER as they move (scan_mark) -- which is
12667               	; 	' what lets both of them fill the band instead of getting a pixel row
12668               	; 	' each. Eight pixels of this canvas is half a screen of the store, so
12669               	; 	' they are almost never in one character; when they are, they merge.
12670               	; 	'
12671               	; 	' Shrinking from six rows bought eight empty pixel rows, four above the
12672               	; 	' instrument and four below, so it no longer butts against the shop floor
12673               	; 	' above it or the bottom of the screen.

13119               	;
13120               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
13121               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
13122               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
13123               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
13124               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
13125               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).
13126               	; scan_wipe:
13127               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
13128               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
13129               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
13130               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
13131               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
13132               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
13133               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
13134               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never

13782               	; #if NES
13783               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
13784               	; 	' Attributes select a palette per 16x16 quadrant. gennescolor.py derives
13785               	; 	' eight screen tables; draw_screen stages one in nesb, masks fixtures,
13786               	; 	' then uploads all 64 bytes through nes_attrs_put within one vblank.
13787               	; 	' A MESSAGE BOX GOES GOLD ON DARK BLUE, and the caller says which four
13788               	; 	' bytes in #nav.
13789               	; 	'
13790               	; 	' The text's paper is index 1 and its ink index 3 (see the font upload);
13791               	; 	' over the store those are P0's green and gold -- the same green the box is
13792               	; 	' sitting on, which is what made the messages hard to read. P1 is the HUD's
13793               	; 	' palette, dark blue and gold, so pointing the box's attribute bytes at it
13794               	; 	' gives a message the same treatment as the score line.
13795               	; 	'
13796               	; 	' FOUR BYTES AND NOT ONE MORE. An attribute byte covers four characters by
13797               	; 	' four, and the box is sized and placed to cover exactly four of them
13798               	; 	' (gentitle.py BOX_ROW/BOX_COL/BOX_W): byte columns 2..5, which is name
13799               	; 	' columns 8..23. Anything wider would recolour shop floor beside the box.
13800               	; 	'
13801               	; 	' THIS IS A ROUTINE BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN OUT TWICE AND MISSED A THIRD
13802               	; 	' TIME. GOT HIM! kept the store's colours while the other boxes changed,
13803               	; 	' and nothing failed -- it is a readable message in the wrong palette.
13804               	; 	' checkmsg.py now fails the build if a message box is drawn without one of
13805               	; 	' these beside it.
13806               	; 	'
13807               	; 	' Nothing puts them back, because nothing needs to: every path out of a
13808               	; 	' message box redraws the screen, and draw_screen calls nes_attr, which
13809               	; 	' rewrites all sixty-four.

14322               	;
14323               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
14324               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
14325               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
14326               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
14327               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
14328               	; 	'
14329               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
14330               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
14331               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
14332               	; 	'
14333               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
14334               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
14335               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
14336               	; 	'
14337               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
14338               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
14339               	; 	'
14340               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
14341               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
14342               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
14343               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
14344               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
14345               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
14346               	; 	'
14347               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
14348               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
14349               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
14350               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
14351               	; 	'
14352               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
14353               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
14354               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
14355               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)
14356               	; bonus_count:
14357               cvb_BONUS_COUNT
14358               	; 	' THE CLOCK IS ABOUT TO BE COUNTED DOWN, so the field has to be up --
14359               	; 	' the round can end on any phase of the low-time flash, and a tally
14360               	; 	' running into a blanked field would draw nothing at all.

14499               	;
14500               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
14501               	; 	'
14502               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
14503               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
14504               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
14505               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
14506               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
14507               	; 	'
14508               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
14509               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
14510               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
14511               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
14512               	; 	' counting stops.
14513               	;
14514               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
14515               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
14516               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
14517               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
14518               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
14519               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
14520               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
14521               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
14522               	; 	'
14523               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
14524               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
14525               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).
14526               	;

14570               	; 	' THE CAST IS NOT TAKEN AWAY YET -- hide_all now runs AFTER the beat.
14571               	; 	'
14572               	; 	' It used to run here, so the moment the clock emptied, Harry and the
14573               	; 	' thing that had just hit him vanished and the sound played over an empty
14574               	; 	' store. The hit that ENDS a round is the worst case: `do_hit` sets tout
14575               	; 	' before the freeze starts and the main loop leaves on the very next pass,
14576               	; 	' so the hit sound gets one tick and everything is already gone.
14577               	; 	'
14578               	; 	' The pause drains the sound; leaving the actors up means it drains over
14579               	; 	' the picture that caused it. Nothing is moving -- the pause ticks sfx_tick
14580               	; 	' and nothing else -- so it is a held tableau, not a frozen game.
14581               	; 	' THE MESSAGE BOX, ON THE GAME SCREEN AND NOT INSTEAD OF IT.
14582               	; 	'
14583               	; 	' It used to CLS before GAME OVER, so the last thing the player saw was
14584               	; 	' the store being deleted and then two words on an empty field -- which
14585               	; 	' reads as the program ending rather than as the game ending. The store
14586               	; 	' stays; the message sits in the middle of it.
14587               	; 	'
14588               	; 	' THE BOX IS THE FONT'S OWN BACKGROUND. Every font character is black on
14589               	; 	' HUD_BG (dark blue), so a row of SPACES is a solid dark blue bar. A blank
14590               	; 	' row above and below the text is a frame for the price of two strings and
14591               	; 	' no new characters, and it reads against the store because nothing else on
14592               	; 	' the playfield is that colour.
14593               	; 	'
14594               	; 	' THIRTEEN WIDE, WHICH IS THE LONGEST MESSAGE PLUS ONE EITHER SIDE.
14595               	; 	' HE GOT AWAY and THE BIPLANE are both eleven. Every string below is padded
14596               	; 	' to exactly thirteen so the box has straight edges, and column 10 puts it
14597               	; 	' at columns 10-22 -- centre 16, the screen's.
14598               	; 	'
14599               	; 	' THE REASON IS ALWAYS ON THE SAME ROW, and that is what lets one layout
14600               	; 	' serve both cases. Losing a life draws three rows around it; losing the
14601               	; 	' last one draws two more ON TOP, so GAME OVER appears above the reason
14602               	; 	' rather than replacing it. Printing the reason at a different row for each
14603               	; 	' case would need `PRINT AT` with a variable, and every other PRINT in this
14604               	; 	' program uses a constant.
14605               	; 	#if NES
14606               	; 	' FLUSH THE PASS BEFORE DRAWING A BOX. PPUBUF accumulates for a whole loop
14607               	; 	' pass and is emptied by one NMI, so a message box -- sixty-four cells,
14608               	; 	' sixty-four single-byte descriptors -- was landing in the same vblank as
14609               	; 	' every radar poke and HUD digit the pass had made. The copy then ran past
14610               	; 	' the end of vblank and the tail was DISCARDED at the PPU: a box with
14611               	; 	' characters missing, and the cut moving from run to run, which is why it
14612               	; 	' read as intermittent corruption.
14613               	; 	'
14614               	; 	' One WAIT here empties the buffer; the box's own writes then self-pace,
14615               	; 	' because WRTVRM waits when PPUBUF fills. That is also why the TITLE never
14616               	; 	' needed this and must not have it: it is drawn at boot with nothing else
14617               	; 	' queued, and a WAIT per run made its twelve runs appear one frame at a
14618               	; 	' time -- a logo that visibly assembled itself.
14619               	; 	WAIT

14873               	;
14874               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
14875               	; 	'
14876               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
14877               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
14878               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
14879               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
14880               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
14881               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
14882               	; 	'
14883               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
14884               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
14885               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
14886               	; 	'
14887               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
14888               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
14889               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
14890               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
14891               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
14892               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
14893               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
14894               	; 	'
14895               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
14896               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
14897               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
14898               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
14899               	; 	'
14900               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
14901               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
14902               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
14903               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
14904               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
14905               	; 	'
14906               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
14907               	; 	' did not finish.
14908               	; pause_beat:

15343               	;
15344               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
15345               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
15346               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
15347               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
15348               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
15349               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
15350               	;
15351               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
15352               	; 	'
15353               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
15354               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
15355               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
15356               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
15357               	; 	'
15358               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
15359               	; 	'
15360               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
15361               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
15362               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
15363               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
15364               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
15365               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
15366               	; 	'
15367               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
15368               	; 	'
15369               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
15370               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
15371               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
15372               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
15373               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
15374               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
15375               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
15376               	; 	'
15377               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
15378               	; 	'
15379               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
15380               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
15381               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
15382               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
15383               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
15384               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
15385               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
15386               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
15387               	; 	'
15388               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
15389               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
15390               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
15391               	; 	'
15392               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
15393               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
15394               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
15395               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
15396               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
15397               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
15398               	; 	'
15399               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
15400               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
15401               	; 	'
15402               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
15403               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
15404               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
15405               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
15406               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
15407               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
15408               	; 	'
15409               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
15410               	; 	'
15411               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
15412               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the
15413               	; 	' whole round. At 13 they were level with the events they are supposed to
15414               	; 	' sit beneath, so the effects that carry information had nothing to stand
15415               	; 	' out from. The tone version was 7 for the same reason -- noise does read
15416               	; 	' quieter than a tone at the same number, which is why this is 9 and not
15417               	; 	' back to 7.

15742               	;
15743               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1 ON THE TI -- the
15744               	; 	' cart's ONE data bank, so the cart is 32 KB (DESIGN.md section 57).
15745               	; 	'
15746               	; 	' It holds the code that runs once or rarely (setup, the title, the 838
15747               	; 	' page, the random level generator, the music hooks) and the two LZSS
15748               	; 	' streams, which lz_setup and lz_probe unpack into lzbuf in RAM. Every
15749               	; 	' table the game reads is read from RAM. Power-on selects the bank once
15750               	; 	' and nothing ever switches it: a missed BANK SELECT returns bytes from
15751               	; 	' the wrong page with no error at build or run time, so the safest
15752               	; 	' number of switches is one.
15753               	; 	'
15754               	; 	' It was two banks and a 64 KB cart until the tables were compressed.
15755               	; 	' A second bank would double the cart again (five pages round up to
15756               	; 	' eight): assets/bankfill.py fails a bank image over 8,192 bytes.
15757               	; 	#if TI994A
15758               	; 	BANK 1
15759      07B4     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$

15793 602E A0FC     	data cls
15794               	; 	' ONE PROMPT AT A TIME, NOTHING ELSE ON THE SCREEN, AND NO NUMBERS UNTIL
15795               	; 	' THEY ARE TYPED. There is no heading and no instructions: a page showing
15796               	; 	' exactly one question does not need to explain that one digit answers it,
15797               	; 	' and the second question does not exist until the first is answered.
15798               	; 	'
15799               	; 	' Showing the CURRENT values first was the obvious thing and it cost more
15800               	; 	' than it gave -- two draw routines, a "fire keeps what is shown" escape to
15801               	; 	' make the display mean something, and the defaults had to be applied here
15802               	; 	' as well as in new_game so the page had numbers to show at all. None of it
15803               	; 	' survives: every digit on screen is one the player just typed. Four
15804               	; 	' strings became two, a two-field loop became a straight line, and the page
15805               	; 	' got SMALLER while getting quieter.

16716               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- GAME MUSIC
16717               	; 	' CHASE (game_tune, genmusic.py) plays during a round on PLAY SIMPLE NO
16718               	; 	' DRUMS: TWO voices on channels 0 and 1 only. The TI effects split by
16719               	; 	' channel -- 0 the jump warble (swt), 1 hits and the escape (sht), 2
16720               	; 	' prizes/lives/tally, noise the footsteps -- so only jumps and hits
16721               	; 	' collide, and those DUCK the music: PLAY NONE freezes the player where
16722               	; 	' it is (it only clears music_mode; the song position is untouched), and
16723               	; 	' PLAY SIMPLE NO DRUMS resumes from the same note once they end.
16724               	; 	'
16725               	; 	' The test runs BEFORE sfx_tick writes anything, and counts the pending
16726               	; 	' latches (sfj/sfh/sfe) as well as the running counters, so the player
16727               	; 	' has let go of the channel before the effect's first write -- otherwise
16728               	; 	' the next vblank would stomp that first frame.
16729               	; 	'
16730               	; 	' Called from the main loop only, never from pause_beat: the round-end
16731               	; 	' pause is effects-only (pause_beat stops the music on entry).
16732               	; 	'
16733               	; 	' ON THE TI IT LIVES IN THE BANK: the fixed area's UNOPTIMISED first
16734               	; 	' pass had 156 bytes left and this body did not fit.
16735               	; music_duck:

16745               	; 	#if NES
16746               	; 	' NES RAM IS FULL TO THE BYTE, so the NES keeps no gms/gmp/gmb: its whole
16747               	; 	' music state is nai -- 0 playing, 1 ducked, 2 not started. nai is NES
16748               	; 	' scratch that is idle here: the title's A toggle uses it (and treats 2
16749               	; 	' like a held A), and the round-end message boxes use it only after the
16750               	; 	' round's music is over and before music_stop sets it back to 2.
16751               	; 	IF nai = 2 THEN nai = 0 : PLAY SIMPLE NO DRUMS : PLAY game_tune
16752               	; 	' Same test as below, branching instead of setting gmb, plus the channel
16753               	; 	' owners the NES adds (the bugle on 0, the prize on 1 -- nes_apu.asm).
16754               	; 	' ONE TEST, NOT NINE. Every one of these is an unsigned byte, so "any is
16755               	; 	' non-zero" is their bitwise OR: one load and eight ORAs, about 35
16756               	; 	' bytes, where nine `IF x > 0 THEN GOTO` cost about 105 on the 6502 --
16757               	; 	' part of what let the NES title play the whole of STREET. (A bitwise OR
16758               	; 	' of VALUES, not of comparisons, so the TI's AND/OR hazard does not
16759               	; 	' apply; and this block is NES-only anyway.)
16760               	; 	IF swt OR sht OR sfj OR sfh OR sfe OR spt OR spz OR sfk OR sfp THEN GOTO md_busy

17049               	; 	' NO ALPHA LOCK CALIBRATION, AND THERE USED TO BE ONE.
17050               	; 	'
17051               	; 	' The premise was that ALPHA LOCK shares a line with the joystick's
17052               	; 	' VERTICAL axis, so a latched key reports a direction that is never
17053               	; 	' released -- fatal here, where down is the duck and up is the lift. The
17054               	; 	' guard sampled the axis for forty frames before listening and then
17055               	; 	' ignored any direction that had been held for essentially all of them.
17056               	; 	'
17057               	; 	' IT WAS REMOVED BECAUSE THE PREMISE DOES NOT HOLD UP.
17058               	; 	'
17059               	; 	'   * CLAUDE.md claimed every other game here dodged the problem by not
17060               	; 	'     reading up/down. EIGHT of them do read it -- Adventire, Astiroids,
17061               	; 	'     HardHatMack, Ms. Pac-Man, RallyX, Structris, UFO, Bust-A-Bobble --
17062               	; 	'     and not one has a calibration or has ever shown the fault.
17063               	; 	'   * It never fired on the machine this is developed on: the notice it
17064               	; 	'     prints when it detects a stuck axis has never appeared.
17065               	; 	'   * The original evidence was that the game "came up and would not
17066               	; 	'     start" -- and the first version BLOCKED until the axis cleared. That
17067               	; 	'     symptom is indistinguishable from the several input bugs since found
17068               	; 	'     and fixed for real: keys arriving at a screen that was not listening
17069               	; 	'     yet. The diagnosis was probably one of those.
17070               	; 	'
17071               	; 	' It also cost two bugs of its own: forty frames of a drawn but deaf title
17072               	; 	' screen, which swallowed the first digit of 8-3-8, and a wrong theory
17073               	; 	' about keyboard noise that led to a filter which ate real presses.
17074               	; 	'
17075               	; 	' If a stuck axis ever does appear it will be obvious -- the player will
17076               	; 	' duck or ride the lift without asking -- and the guard is in the history.

17136               	; 	' THE MARQUEE CHASES WHILE THE TITLE WAITS.
17137               	; 	'
17138               	; 	' ONLY TWO CHARACTERS CHANGE PER STEP. At any moment exactly one of the
17139               	; 	' four lamps is blank; a step lights the one that was blank and blanks the
17140               	; 	' next one round. Redefining all four would be twice the work for the same
17141               	; 	' picture.
17142               	; 	'
17143               	; 	' IT IS BELOW THE INPUT READS, deliberately. This loop's history is input
17144               	; 	' bugs -- a screen that was drawn but not listening, a keypress eaten by a
17145               	; 	' stability filter -- so nothing that is merely decoration goes in front of
17146               	; 	' the polling. A dropped frame of animation is invisible; a dropped
17147               	; 	' keypress is what took three sessions to find.
17148               	; 	' `bphs` IS WHICH LAMP IS DARK, and a step is: light that one, move on,
17149               	; 	' darken the next. The character number is arithmetic rather than a
17150               	; 	' four-way branch -- DEFINE CHAR takes an expression, so the whole chase
17151               	; 	' is two calls and no `IF` ladder. The ladder version was eight DEFINE
17152               	; 	' CHARs across four branches and cost about three hundred bytes for the
17153               	; 	' same picture.
17154               	; 	'
17155               	; 	' TWO CALLS, NOT FIVE. Lighting all four and then darkening one is the
17156               	; 	' same result and reads more simply, but two separate DEFINEs can have a
17157               	; 	' vblank between them, so the sign would show ALL lamps lit for a frame
17158               	; 	' every step -- a flash rather than a chase. Only ever changing the two
17159               	; 	' lamps that actually change cannot do that.
17160               	; 	bfr = bfr - 1

17227               	; 		#if NES
17228               	; 		' A SECOND STAGING AREA, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE MARQUEE BUG.
17229               	; 		'
17230               	; 		' nes_escd does NOT copy anything. It builds the tile into the RAM
17231               	; 		' buffer `#nesb` and hands the NMI a five-byte descriptor holding a
17232               	; 		' POINTER to it; the copy happens at the next vblank. Both marquee
17233               	; 		' writes happen in the same pass, so with one buffer the darken call
17234               	; 		' overwrote the staged LIT bytes before the NMI had read either --
17235               	; 		' and then BOTH descriptors copied bulb_off.
17236               	; 		'
17237               	; 		' So every step darkened two lamps and lit none, and the sign walked
17238               	; 		' itself out: "it animates a little bit and goes out". Nothing fails,
17239               	; 		' because both writes are perfectly valid and land exactly where they
17240               	; 		' were addressed -- they just carry the same sixteen bytes.
17241               	; 		'
17242               	; 		' The lit call staged at nesb(0); this one stages sixteen bytes up.
17243               	; 		' nesb is 96 bytes for the escalator's six characters and the
17244               	; 		' escalator never runs on the title screen, so the room is free. The
17245               	; 		' pointer is put back immediately: esc_tick stages at offset 0 and
17246               	; 		' would otherwise write its six characters one tile off.

17485               	;
17486               	; 	' 8-3-8 IS EDGE-TRIGGERED AND ANY STRAY DIGIT RESETS IT (see title_wait).
17487               	; 	'
17488               	; 	' It used to read cont1.key raw every pass and test only for the digit it
17489               	; 	' wanted next. That worked -- but only because 8-3-8 ALTERNATES, so holding
17490               	; 	' 8 cannot advance past the first step. It is an accident of the sequence
17491               	; 	' rather than a design, and it had two costs: 8,5,3,9,8 opened this page as
17492               	; 	' readily as 8,3,8, and a key that READS as held for many frames got a free
17493               	; 	' walk through the state machine.
17494               	; 	'
17495               	; 	' That second one is not hypothetical on this machine. ALPHA LOCK shorts a
17496               	; 	' keyboard line -- and Classic99 defaults to invertcaps, so it reads DOWN
17497               	; 	' with the host's Caps Lock UP -- and this page was reached twice from
17498               	; 	' single keypresses while testing an unrelated change.
17499               	; 	'
17500               	; 	' The reset is the DEFAULT rather than a test for a particular wrong digit:
17501               	; 	' Bust-A-Bobble resets only on a stray 3 and still lets 8,5,3,8 through.
17502               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------------- 838 setup page
17503               	; 	' ======================================================================
17504               	; 	' A NEW GAME / A NEW KROOK
17505               	; 	' ======================================================================
17506               	;
17507               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- RUN ONCE
17508               	; 	' setup_font and init_tables run ONCE, at power-on, so on the TI they live
17509               	; 	' in the bank. They moved out of the fixed area to make room for the TI
17510               	; 	' music player (title music, ~1.2 KB of runtime): with it, the
17511               	; 	' UNOPTIMISED first assembly ran past >FFFF and xas99 rejected branches
17512               	; 	' before shortbranches.py could run (CLAUDE.md 3A, TI short-branch note).
17513               	; 	' On ColecoVision and NES this is ordinary code.
17514               	; setup_font:
17515               cvb_SETUP_FONT
17516               	; 	' Flicker stays OFF. CVBasic's is all-or-nothing -- it rotates all 32
17517               	; 	' slots, so Kelly would strobe too, and he is the one thing the player
17518               	; 	' must never lose. He is sprite 0 instead: the VDP drops the
17519               	; 	' HIGHEST-numbered sprites on an over-full scanline, so slot 0 is the
17520               	; 	' one slot that can never disappear.
17521               	; 	SPRITE FLICKER OFF
17522 6B06 0200  20 	li r0,>0400
     6B08 0400     
17523 6B0A F800  30 	socb r0,@mode
     6B0C 834E     
17524               	;
17525               	; 	#if NES
17526               	; 	' No BORDER on this machine: the area outside the picture is the backdrop,
17527               	; 	' palette entry 0, which title_draw and draw_screen already set.
17528               	; 	#else
17529               	; 	' DARK BLUE, NOT BLACK. The TMS border is the strip outside the 256x192
17530               	; 	' picture, and on a real set it is a good part of what the player sees --
17531               	; 	' left at the default black it made a hard frame around the shop. Dark blue
17532               	; 	' is the sky's own colour and the paper every piece of text sits on, so the
17533               	; 	' picture runs out to the edge of the tube instead of stopping at it.
17534               	; 	BORDER 4
17535 6B0E 0200  20 	li r0,1024   ; 4*256
     6B10 0400     
17536 6B12 0980  32 	srl r0,8

     6B16 8700

17539 6B1A 0300  22 	limi 0
     6B1C 0000     
17540 6B1E D800  30 	movb r0,@VDPWADR
     6B20 8C02     
17541 6B22 06C0  14 	swpb r0
17542 6B24 D800  30 	movb r0,@VDPWADR
     6B26 8C02     
17543 6B28 0300  22 	limi 2
     6B2A 0002     
17544               	; 	#endif
17545               	;
17546               	; 	#if NES
17547               	; 	' THE NES'S TWO STRUCTURAL DIFFERENCES, SETTLED ONCE, HERE.
17548               	; 	'
17549               	; 	' 1. WHERE THE PATTERNS LIVE. In 8x16 sprite mode the sprite pattern table
17550               	; 	'    is chosen by bit 0 of each OAM tile byte and the PPUCTRL bit is
17551               	; 	'    ignored -- and every pattern number in this game is a multiple of
17552               	; 	'    four, so that bit is always 0 and the sprites are nailed to $0000.
17553               	; 	'    nes_bgbank therefore moves the BACKGROUND to $1000 rather than trying
17554               	; 	'    to move the sprites, which also lands the background patterns at
17555               	; 	'    address 4096, exactly where the TMS bitmap mode's third screen third
17556               	; 	'    had them -- so the radar's pattern writes need a stride and nothing
17557               	; 	'    else.
17558               	; 	'
17559               	; 	' 2. COLOUR DOES NOT MAP AND IS NOT PRETENDED TO. The NES colours in 16x16
17560               	; 	'    attribute blocks; this game colours per character, two colours a
17561               	; 	'    cell. So the store is drawn in ONE ink and the actors get four
17562               	; 	'    palettes, picked by the low two bits of the colour argument the
17563               	; 	'    SPRITE statements already pass -- 1 (black) -> dark grey, 4/8 (blue)
17564               	; 	'    -> blue, 14 (grey) -> grey, 11/15 (skin, white) -> white. Nothing in
17565               	; 	'    the game source has to know.
17566               	; 	ASM JSR nes_bgbank
17567               	; 	ASM JSR nes_apuon
17568               	;
17569               	; 	' Grey is shared index 0 during gameplay. Other indices are per region.
17570               	; 	' gennescolor.py assigns P3 only to counter quadrants, retaining green
17571               	; 	' wall and gold floor colours. Fixtures with black outlines use P0.
17572               	; 	PALETTE 1,26			' P0: green, black, gold
17573               	; 	PALETTE 2,15			' black escalators and fixture outlines
17574               	; 	PALETTE 3,40
17575               	; 	PALETTE 5,1			' P1 HUD/upper skyline: blue, pink, gold
17576               	; 	PALETTE 6,36
17577               	; 	PALETTE 7,40
17578               	; 	PALETTE 9,38			' P2 lower skyline: orange, black, gold
17579               	; 	PALETTE 10,1			' unused skyline index 2: navy message bottom border
17580               	; 	PALETTE 11,40
17581               	; 	PALETTE 13,26			' P3 counters: green, blue, gold
17582               	; 	PALETTE 14,1			' same navy in counter quadrants
17583               	; 	PALETTE 15,40
17584               	;
17585               	; 	' AND FOUR FOR THE ACTORS, which DO get one each because a sprite carries
17586               	; 	' its own palette number. nes_spal maps the TMS colour every SPRITE
17587               	; 	' statement already passes onto these four.
17588               	; 	PALETTE 17,18			' 0 -- blue   Kelly's trousers
17589               	; 	PALETTE 21,15			' 1 -- black  hats, Harry's stripes, the Kop's dot.
17590               	; 					' FIFTEEN, NOT ZERO: on this palette $0F is
17591               	; 					' black and $00 is a dark GREY, so every hat
17592               	; 					' and every stripe was coming out grey.
17593               	; 	PALETTE 22,23			' black sprite palette, index 2: brown suitcase outline
17594               	; 	PALETTE 25,39			' 2 -- skin   faces and the biplane
17595               	; 	PALETTE 26,16			' 2 colour 2 -- GREY, the lift car on the radar
17596               	; 	' AND THE BALL IS RED, which it already is on the TI: C_BALL is TMS 8,
17597               	; 	' medium red. nes_spal sends that to sprite palette 2, and palette 2's
17598               	; 	' colour ONE is the skin tone -- so on this machine the ball came out the
17599               	; 	' same pale orange as a face.
17600               	; 	'
17601               	; 	' A sprite here is ONE bitplane, so its pixels are whichever index the
17602               	; 	' upload writes and the OAM byte only chooses the palette. The lift car on
17603               	; 	' the radar already solved this: it is uploaded with `nink = 2` and reads
17604               	; 	' palette 2's second entry. The ball does the same with the THIRD, which
17605               	; 	' nothing else uses.
17606               	; 	PALETTE 27,22			' 2 colour 3 -- RED, the bouncing balls
17607               	; 	PALETTE 29,48			' 3 -- white  Harry, the carts, the lift car
17608               	;
17609               	; 	#endif
17610               	; 	#if TI994A
17611               	; 	#else
17612               	; 	nespw = 2			' NES/Coleco start on a 2-frame pass
17613               	; 	#endif
17614               	;
17615               	; 	' THE FONTS COME FROM lzbuf ON THE TI: lz_setup unpacked the setup
17616               	; 	' tables there at power-on, before this runs (DESIGN.md section 55).
17617               	; 	' If that ever goes wrong it goes wrong loudly -- the title's text is
17618               	; 	' garbage, immediately and unmistakably.
17619               	;
17620               	; 	#if NES
17621               	; 	' THE FONT IS SENT WITH A COLOUR TABLE SO ITS PAPER IS NOT THE BACKDROP.
17622               	; 	'
17623               	; 	' With `#ncol = 0` the uploader puts ink `nink` on index 0 -- the UNIVERSAL
17624               	; 	' backdrop, black in the game -- so every character of text sat in its own
17625               	; 	' black box. The score line was a black strip across the top of a blue sky.
17626               	; 	'
17627               	; 	' Index 0 cannot be set per region (it is one colour for the whole screen),
17628               	; 	' so the only way to give text a ground is to put its PAPER on another
17629               	; 	' index, and paper is written into the second bitplane when the character
17630               	; 	' is uploaded. Hence a table: $B4 is light yellow on dark blue, which
17631               	; 	' nes_inkmap sends to index 3 and index 1.
17632               	; 	'
17633               	; 	' ONE FONT, NOT TWO. The first attempt at this made a SECOND copy of the
17634               	; 	' font at codes 197.. so the HUD could differ from the message boxes, and
17635               	; 	' that was both unnecessary and impossible: in game the HUD and the boxes
17636               	; 	' are the same text and want the same treatment, and 197..207 is only
17637               	; 	' ELEVEN free codes -- 208 up is the radar canvas (genart's SCAN_FIRST),
17638               	; 	' which scan_wipe rewrites as raw pattern memory every frame. The 59-char
17639               	; 	' copy appeared to upload and was scribbled over from its twelfth character
17640               	; 	' on. See checkpat.py, which now knows the canvas owns those codes.
17641               	; 	'
17642               	; 	' What index 1 IS comes from the attribute table, per region: the HUD row
17643               	; 	' is on P1 (dark blue, below) and the store is on P0.
17644               	; 	#nsrc = VARPTR font_bits(0)
17645               	; 	nchr = 32
17646               	; 	ncnt = 59
17647               	; 	ntab = 1
17648               	; 	' THE FONT'S COLOUR, $B4 on every row of all 59 characters: light yellow
17649               	; 	' on dark blue, ink index 3 on paper index 1, and which colours those are
17650               	; 	' is then the attribute table's business, per region. It used to be a
17651               	; 	' 472-byte table of that one value (nes_fcol), kept because "ROM is not
17652               	; 	' the scarce budget" -- on the NES it is. A #ncol under $100 is the
17653               	; 	' colour byte itself (assets/nes_chr.asm, nes_chrinkrow).
17654               	; 	#ncol = $B4
17655               	; 	nink = 3
17656               	; 	GOSUB nes_def
17657               	; 	#else
17658               	; 	DEFINE CHAR 32,59,font_bits
17659 6B2C 0204  20 	li r4,32
     6B2E 0020     
17660 6B30 0205  20 	li r5,15104
     6B32 3B00     
17661 6B34 0200  20 	li r0,cvb_FONT_BITS
     6B36 3034     
17662 6B38 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     6B3A AE2A     
17663 6B3C A1FA     	data define_char
17664               	; 	#endif
17665               	; 	' Without this the font keeps whatever CVBasic left in the colour table --
17666               	; 	' white on transparent -- which over a green store made the HUD unreadable.
17667               	; 	'
17668               	; 	' THIS WAS A VPOKE LOOP AND IT WAS THE SLOWEST THING IN THE BOOT: 1,416
17669               	; 	' writes of one constant, paced by 24 WAITs, which is what made the title
17670               	; 	' fill in visibly instead of appearing. DEFINE COLOR does the same job in a
17671               	; 	' single call with interrupts off, and it writes all three screen thirds
17672               	; 	' itself -- define_color always takes the LDIRVM3 triple-copy path, which is
17673               	; 	' also why esc_deck_col and floor0_colour below CANNOT use it: they patch
17674               	; 	' one third each.
17675               	; 	'
17676               	; 	' The table is 472 identical bytes (genfont.py emits it beside the glyphs).
17677               	; 	' It reads as waste and is not: it lives in the data bank, which had 860
17678               	; 	' bytes spare, while the loop it replaced cost time in the one place the
17679               	; 	' player is made to wait.
17680               	; 	#if NES
17681               	; 	' no colour table on this machine -- see nes_setup
17682               	; 	#else
17683               	; 	DEFINE COLOR 32,59,font_col
17684 6B3E 0204  20 	li r4,32
     6B40 0020     
17685 6B42 0205  20 	li r5,15104
     6B44 3B00     
17686 6B46 0200  20 	li r0,cvb_FONT_COL
     6B48 320C     
17687 6B4A 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     6B4C AE2A     
17688 6B4E A22E     	data define_color
17689               	; 	#endif
17690               	;
17691               	; 	' AND THE TITLE'S DISPLAY FACE, WHICH IS HERE FOR THE SAME REASON THE
17692               	; 	' FONT IS. Forty characters -- ten letters, four cells each -- drawn at
17693               	; 	' 16x16 so the game's name reads as a name rather than as a line of body
17694               	; 	' text. It is 640 bytes of pattern and colour and bank 1 had 370 free, so
17695               	; 	' it could not go there; it did not need to, because it is read ONCE, by
17696               	; 	' these two statements, and never again.
17697               	; 	'
17698               	; 	' On the TI it is in lzbuf with the other setup tables.
17699               	; 	' IN TWO PIECES, AND THE SPLIT IS NOT TIDINESS. The character table has
17700               	; 	' 0..31, 91..95 and 182..207 free -- sixty-three codes, but the longest
17701               	; 	' run is thirty-two and the face needs forty. Loading it as one block at
17702               	; 	' 182 ran it into the RADAR CANVAS at 208, and S and T came out as the

17923               	; 	' THE JUMP ARC IS A TABLE, not integration. That makes the 14 px apex a
17924               	; 	' property of the data rather than of a fixed-point velocity that has to
17925               	; 	' be tuned, and it keeps every comparison in the jump 8-bit and unsigned.
17926               	; 	' DESIGN.md 5a depends on the apex being exactly 14.
17927               	; 	'
17928               	; 	' THIRTY FRAMES WITH NINE OF THEM AT THE APEX. The first version was 24
17929               	; 	' frames that touched 14 for only four, which made every jump a timing
17930               	; 	' test rather than a decision -- you had to leave the ground on exactly
17931               	; 	' the right frame or clip the thing you were jumping. Widening the
17932               	; 	' plateau rather than raising the apex keeps the ball arithmetic in
17933               	; 	' DESIGN.md 5a intact (the apex is what that depends on) while making the
17934               	; 	' window forgiving: the player still has to CHOOSE to jump, but no longer
17935               	; 	' has to be frame-perfect about it.
17936               	; 	' THE ARC IS A TABLE, not thirty assignments -- each of those compiled to

17971               	;
17972               	; 	' THE FONT'S COLOUR TABLE WAS 472 BYTES OF ONE REPEATED VALUE, which is a
17973               	; 	' fifth of what the fixed area had left. DEFINE COLOR copies such a table
17974               	; 	' out of ROM into all three screen thirds; writing the constant straight
17975               	; 	' into the colour table does the same job for the price of a loop, and
17976               	; 	' the loop runs once, at boot.
17977               	; 	'
17978               	; 	' The colour table is at >2000 and the VDP mirrors it once per screen
17979               	; 	' third, >800 apart. Both numbers were read out of the GENERATED assembly
17980               	; 	' -- define_color's `ai r0,>2000` and LDIRVM3's `ai r0,>0800` -- rather
17981               	; 	' than assumed, because a wrong base here would paint over the pattern
17982               	; 	' table and the failure would look like corrupt artwork.
17983               	; 	'
17984               	; 	' Paced: a few hundred VDP writes in one frame are silently dropped.
17985               	; 	' THE SCANNER'S COLOURS ARE THREE BLOCKS REPEATED SIXTEEN TIMES EACH, so
17986               	; 	' the table shipped 384 bytes to say 24 bytes' worth. Same trick as the
17987               	; 	' font: write the colour table directly. >2000 is the colour table's base
17988               	; 	' and >800 the stride between screen thirds -- the same layout DEFINE COLOR
17989               	; 	' walks for us in setup_font, which this cannot use because it is cheaper to
17990               	; 	' expand 24 bytes here than to ship 384 in the bank.
17991               	; 	' NOTHING IS UNDER THE GROUND FLOOR, SO NOTHING SHOULD BE GREEN THERE.
17992               	; 	' A floor bar is five pixels of yellow over three of the green air
17993               	; 	' belonging to the floor BELOW it (see SLAB), which is right for three of
17994               	; 	' the four bars and wrong for the last one: below floor 0 there is no
17995               	; 	' floor, only the scanner, and the green read as a strip of shop with
17996               	; 	' nothing in it.
17997               	; 	'
17998               	; 	' NO NEW CHARACTER IS NEEDED, BECAUSE THE COLOUR TABLE HAS THREE COPIES
17999               	; 	' -- one per eight screen rows -- and the bands land such that each bar
18000               	; 	' sits in a different third:
18001               	; 	'
18002               	; 	'     band 0 roof   rows  1-5    bar row  5   third 0
18003               	; 	'     band 1        rows  6-10   bar row 10   third 1
18004               	; 	'     band 2        rows 11-15   bar row 15   third 1
18005               	; 	'     band 3 GROUND rows 16-20   bar row 20   third 2
18006               	; 	'
18007               	; 	' so recolouring SLAB in third 2 alone reaches the ground floor's bar and
18008               	; 	' nothing else. The same third also holds the scanner, but the scanner
18009               	; 	' does not use these characters. This is the same mechanism that once hid
18010               	; 	' a bug for months (CLAUDE.md 3A, the blanked-in-one-third note) used
18011               	; 	' deliberately for once.
18012               	; 	'
18013               	; 	' Only the three bottom lines change, and only their BACKGROUND: SLAB has
18014               	; 	' no ink there and SLABE's brick keeps its grey.
18015               	;
18016               	; 	INCLUDE "font.bas"
18017               	; 	' Keystone Kapers font -- GENERATED by assets/genfont.py. Do not edit; regenerate.
18018               	; 	'
18019               	; 	' Characters 32-90 (59 of them), 8 bytes each = 472 bytes. Williams' cabinet face:
18020               	; 	' heavy, squared, flat terminals, no serifs -- drawn 5x7 inside the 8x8 cell so a
18021               	; 	' blank column at the right and a blank row at the bottom keep it legible.
18022               	; 	'
18023               	; 	' Loaded with DEFINE CHAR 32,59,font_bits. The run must be CONTIGUOUS, so slots
18024               	; 	' with no glyph emit blanks rather than being skipped -- a gap would shift every
18025               	; 	' letter after it.
18026               	;
18027               	; #if TI994A
18028               	; #else
18029               	; font_bits:
18030               	; 	DATA BYTE $00,$00,$00,$00,$00,$00,$00,$00	' space
18031               	; 	DATA BYTE $20,$20,$20,$20,$20,$00,$20,$00	' !
18032               	; 	DATA BYTE $00,$00,$38,$04,$3C,$44,$3C,$00	' "
18033               	; 	DATA BYTE $04,$04,$3C,$44,$44,$44,$3C,$00	' #
18034               	; 	DATA BYTE $00,$00,$38,$44,$7C,$40,$38,$00	' $
18035               	; 	DATA BYTE $30,$10,$10,$10,$10,$10,$38,$00	' %
18036               	; 	DATA BYTE $60,$90,$A0,$40,$A8,$90,$68,$00	' &
18037               	; 	DATA BYTE $20,$20,$00,$00,$00,$00,$00,$00	' '
18038               	; 	DATA BYTE $00,$00,$78,$44,$78,$40,$40,$40	' (
18039               	; 	DATA BYTE $00,$00,$58,$64,$40,$40,$40,$00	' )
18040               	; 	DATA BYTE $00,$00,$88,$50,$20,$50,$88,$00	' *
18041               	; 	DATA BYTE $00,$00,$3C,$40,$38,$04,$78,$00	' +
18042               	; 	DATA BYTE $00,$00,$78,$44,$44,$44,$44,$00	' ,
18043               	; 	DATA BYTE $00,$00,$00,$F8,$00,$00,$00,$00	' -
18044               	; 	DATA BYTE $00,$00,$00,$00,$00,$60,$60,$00	' .
18045               	; 	DATA BYTE $08,$08,$10,$20,$40,$80,$80,$00	' /
18046               	; 	DATA BYTE $70,$88,$98,$A8,$C8,$88,$70,$00	' 0
18047               	; 	DATA BYTE $20,$60,$20,$20,$20,$20,$70,$00	' 1
18048               	; 	DATA BYTE $70,$88,$08,$30,$40,$80,$F8,$00	' 2

20728               	; 	' ---------------------------------------------------------------- LZSS (TI)
20729               	; 	' THE DECODER for assets/lzss.py's format: a flag byte governs eight items,
20730               	; 	' least significant bit first; 1 = a literal byte, 0 = a two-byte match,
20731               	; 	' big-endian (offset << 6 | length - 3), offset 1..1023 back into the
20732               	; 	' output. #lzs = the compressed stream, #lzd = the RAM destination, #lzn =
20733               	; 	' the output length (it stops there, so a stream's padding is never read).
20734               	; 	' R1-R9 only: R10 is CVBasic's stack pointer and R11 its return link.
20735               	; 	' It lives in BANK 1 with its stream, which must be selected (power-on
20736               	; 	' selects it before calling lz_probe), and needs no fixed-area room.
